165.bp: When we want machines to understand networks—social graphs, molecule structures, citation webs—we need them to learn useful patterns without human labels. Unsupervised learning (learning on data nobody has hand-marked as right or wrong) can be powerful because you don't need expensive human annotation, but the challenge is figuring out what patterns are actually worth learning.
165.wh: The core tension: in a real network, you could describe the same node or subgraph from many viewpoints—its direct neighbors, its broader community, its role in the whole graph. Standard methods either focus on one viewpoint or glue them together crudely. When you do that, you either miss rich diversity or get confused signals that pull against each other. And you need to balance internal consistency (things nearby should be treated similarly) with flexibility (rigid rules overfit). Without addressing this at multiple scales—individual nodes, small groups, the whole graph—you lose signal.
165.ap: The method starts by creating multiple 'views' of the graph using a diffusion matrix (a mathematical object that spreads influence smoothly across the network). This gives different angles on the same graph. Then it feeds all these views through an asymmetric neural network—different pathways for different views, not forced into one mold—so each can develop its own specialized features. Finally, it uses a three-level contrastive loss: at the node level, at the subgraph level, and at the whole-graph level. Contrastive learning works by making the model pull similar things closer and push dissimilar things apart, training it to capture what makes things alike or different.
165.ww: Why does this work? First, the diffusion matrix creates mathematically smooth variations rather than arbitrary crops, so you're seeing the same network from genuinely different angles, not just noise. Second, asymmetric pathways let each view develop its own strengths without a single bottleneck. Third, and crucially, training at three scales forces the model to learn consistent patterns across granularities: if node-level and global patterns contradict, you'll catch it. The temperature coefficient acts like a tuning knob—it calibrates how sharply the model discriminates between similar and dissimilar things.
165.po: On node and graph classification tasks across multiple benchmark datasets, the model achieves high accuracy. The payoff is concrete: you can classify nodes in a social network or whole molecular graphs with strong performance using only unlabeled data. This matters because labeled graph datasets are expensive to build, especially for specialized domains like chemistry or biology.

166.bp: Recommender systems that understand 'what you want next' need to remember your entire history—every video you watched, every song you clicked. But processing years of history is computationally expensive. The real-world goal: give you a better recommendation by knowing your long-term patterns without making the server collapse under the weight of it all.
166.wh: Here's the trap: your history is very long (thousands of items) but the server can only process so much. Existing shortcuts take two approaches, each broken in its own way. Compression methods (split history into chunks and summarize each) work fast but they create artificial boundaries: they might slice apart items that belong together temporally, or lose the texture of how your interests flow smoothly over time. Retrieval methods (pick only the 'most relevant' past items) preserve continuity but throw away too much context—you lose the surrounding story that explains *why* something is relevant. It's lose-lose: compress and break time-flow, retrieve and go blind to context.
166.ap: The paper proposes balancing both. Rather than pure compression or pure retrieval, it uses adaptive subsequence compression: chunk your history in a way that respects temporal proximity (items close in time stay together) while also respecting item similarity (similar things can be grouped). Then it adds contextual fusion, which brings back some of the discarded context during the learning phase, so the model can see both the focused retrieved items and their surrounding context. It's like reading the full paragraph around a highlighted sentence instead of just the highlight.
166.ww: This works because you're doing two things simultaneously: reducing the computational load (so servers don't slow down) and preserving both the temporal structure (the natural flow of your interests over time) and the context (why one recommendation connects to another). Adaptive chunking finds the natural breaks in your history rather than forcing uniform segments. Contextual fusion means the model learns from the relevant core *and* its neighborhood, so it understands both what matters and why.
166.po: In practice: the system processes much longer user histories than existing methods can handle, giving better recommendations that account for long-term patterns. This enables 'lifelong' recommendation—services that improve over years of data without asking you to re-train constantly or trimming your history.

167.bp: Live video streaming (think Twitch, YouTube Live, sports broadcasts) reaches hundreds of millions of people and must arrive with minimal delay. The network carrying this video constantly changes—congestion comes and goes unpredictably. The goal: send video as smoothly as possible without buffering, using the available bandwidth fully, even when conditions shift moment-to-moment.
167.wh: The paradox at the heart of this paper: the video encoder produces frames of wildly different sizes. One frame might encode as 50KB, the next as 500KB. Current congestion control algorithms work at the packet level—they look at individual data packets arriving at network bottlenecks and estimate available bandwidth from that. But if a huge frame shows up suddenly and you're sending at the wrong rate, you either lose packets (causing glitches) or delay them (causing buffering). The algorithm doesn't see the frame-size jumps coming, so it can't anticipate the sending pattern that the encoder will actually demand.
167.ap: The paper introduces Camel, which operates at the frame level instead of the packet level. It watches when frames finish encoding and estimates network capacity from how those frames flow through the network, not from individual packets. Camel has three parts: (1) a bandwidth and delay estimator that looks at frame-by-frame network behavior to understand true available capacity, (2) a congestion detector that notices when the network gets overwhelmed, and (3) a burst controller that decides when it's safe to send a large frame in one rush versus spreading it out. The key insight: frame-level signals are more stable and predictive than packet-level noise.
167.ww: Frame-level feedback works because video encoders output frames as atomic units. If you estimate capacity from how frames traverse the network, you're measuring something the encoder actually produces and the network actually carries. You're not being fooled by packet-level timing jitter that has nothing to do with true capacity. The burst controller prevents the classic problem: a huge frame arrives, you're still using old estimates, you send too fast, packets queue up, latency spikes, stream stalls. Instead, you know the frame size in advance and have real network feedback to modulate the sending pattern.
167.po: Real-world deployment at a major platform: 250 million users, 2 billion sessions, 150+ countries. The payoff is measurable: fewer stalling events and smoother video delivery. Video streaming is latency-sensitive (people notice 100ms delays), so frame-level control that prevents sudden queueing spikes translates directly to better viewing experience.

168.bp: Organizations need to catch insider threats—employees or contractors doing something malicious (stealing data, sabotaging systems, spying). The catch is that malicious actions are rare and hidden in mountains of normal-looking behavior. You might track user logins, file access, network activity, email—many different 'views' of what someone does. The goal: combine all these signals to spot the small fraction of dangerous activity.
168.wh: Naive fusion fails in three ways. First, if you train a separate model for each data type (logins, files, email), then try to combine them, you either have scalability chaos (retraining everything each time you add a new signal) or semantic garbage (the models were trained on different things and their outputs don't align). Second, when signals do align, they often pull in different strengths: video analytics might be excellent at detecting abnormal mouse movement but useless at email, while email models catch linguistic red flags that video can't see. Simple averaging drowns out the weaker but valuable signals. Third, insider threat data is imbalanced: 99.99% normal, 0.01% threats. Rare classes get ignored unless you're careful.
168.ap: Insight-LLM is a multi-view fusion framework. Each view (logins, files, email, etc.) gets encoded by a pre-trained model kept frozen—no retraining overhead. A lightweight adapter aligns all these heterogeneous representations into one shared semantic space, like translating everything to a common language. Then a context-adaptive fusion module learns to re-weight views dynamically: for this particular user interaction, maybe email patterns matter most; for another, file access does. Finally, the fused representation is combined with a task description and fed to a lightweight language model for final threat classification.
168.ww: This works because frozen pre-trained models are free (they're already trained), so adding new views is cheap. The ViewAdapter solves semantic misalignment by learning a small transformation per view, not retraining everything. Dynamic re-weighting prevents strong views from drowning out weak ones—each view gets a chance to speak up when it has signal. The language model acts as a final reasoning step, able to synthesize complex combinations ('this user's file access pattern is weird *and* their email mentions financial stress—flag it'). Because you keep models trained separately, adding a new signal doesn't ripple through the entire system.
168.po: On real insider threat datasets: F1 score (accuracy at catching threats without false alarms) improves up to 4.8%, and false-positive rate drops 61%. That means fewer innocent employees get flagged, and more actual threats get caught. Retraining time per new signal also drops sharply, so you can adapt to new types of threat quickly.

169.bp: When large language models interact with users—answering questions, following instructions, potentially being manipulated—there's a trail of evidence: the prompt someone sent and the response the model gave. If the model does something wrong (gives unsafe advice, leaks data, gets tricked), traditional digital forensics doesn't help; you need to investigate the LLM interaction itself. The goal: audit and reconstruct what happened, who asked what, and whether the model behaved safely.
169.wh: Traditional digital forensics looks at deleted files, server logs, network packets. But LLM interactions are different: they're designed to be transient and fast, not logged by default. If you want to audit whether a model was 'jailbroken' (tricked into ignoring safety rules) or produced unsafe output, you need a chain of evidence: what was the exact prompt, what was the exact response, can you replay it, and can you diagnose where it went wrong? But current LLM systems don't provide this in a forensically rigorous way—logs get overwritten, exact prompts aren't always preserved, and there's no principled way to replay a specific interaction.
169.ap: Prompt Forensics introduces Prompt Scene Investigation (PSI): three forensic procedures from classical crime-scene investigation applied to LLM safety. (1) Prompt Processing captures every interaction as a tamper-resistant ID—like a digital chain of custody in a criminal case, where you log exactly what you found and when, so later no one can claim it was altered. (2) Replay re-runs the model with the exact same prompt under controlled conditions, isolating what the model is doing from surrounding variables. (3) Investigation uses these replays to detect adversarial attacks and policy violations, producing diagnostic reports: 'this prompt uses technique X to bypass safety guard Y, and the model responded with Z.'
169.ww: This works because it's structured as evidence gathering, not arbitrary logging. Tamper-resistant IDs create accountability (if someone claims the log is fake, you can verify the chain). Replay isolates causation: you see exactly what the model does when given a specific input, controlling for randomness and other factors. Diagnostic reports connect the dots from prompt to response to violation, making the 'what went wrong' observable and debuggable. It's modeled on forensics because auditing safety is fundamentally about reconstructing past events from traces.
169.po: The payoff: regulatory compliance and incident response. If an LLM produces harmful output, you can now audit it: prove what was asked, prove what was answered, prove whether it violated policy, and diagnose the failure mode. This enables accountability for AI systems in high-stakes domains (healthcare, finance, government) where forensic evidence matters legally.

170.bp: Imagine shopping: you find a picture of boots you like, but you want a different color and maybe a thicker heel. You combine the reference image with text describing the change. A search system needs to find boots that match this composite query—not just similar to the original image, but reflecting the textual modifications too. Real goal: understand that the query is asking for something partially seen (the image) and partially imagined (the text modifications).
170.wh: Standard similarity-based search fails because it treats the reference image and text as separate things to average or concatenate. But the query is actually compositional: the image defines a base, and the text describes edits. A system might find images similar to the boots (same style) while ignoring the color change, or find the right color but lose the style. The deeper problem: you need both semantic reasoning ('does this match the modified description?') and visual verification ('does it actually look right?'). Most training-based methods get stuck in one modality and miss cross-modal reasoning.
170.ap: XR orchestrates multiple specialized AI agents working together. Imagination agents synthesize what the target should look like by combining the image and text into a generated representation. Similarity agents do coarse filtering by hybrid matching—they look at both visual and textual similarity, checking rough fit. Question agents verify by targeted reasoning: they ask specific questions like 'is this the right color?' and 'does the style match?' and check the answers against the original query. These three types of agents work iteratively and progressively refine the results: imagination makes a guess, similarity filters to the likely set, questions check consistency, and repeat.
170.ww: This works because each agent handles what it does best. Imagination agents leverage cross-modal generation (they've seen many image-text pairs and can synthesize what a modified version should look like). Similarity agents do fast geometric filtering (comparing vectors in a space where both images and text concepts exist). Question agents do verification by semantic reasoning (they can check whether 'bright red' actually matches 'crimson' or whether 'thicker heel' is satisfied). By coordinating these rather than trying to do everything in one model, the system gets the benefits of generative reasoning, efficient filtering, and semantic verification without training from scratch.
170.po: On three benchmark datasets (FashionIQ, CIRR, CIRCO), the method achieves up to 38% improvement over strong baselines without requiring any task-specific training. The payoff: users can query with 'show me boots like these but taller and in suede' and get exactly what they mean, not just vague similarity matches.

171.bp: Question-answering systems usually extract or generate answers that appear somewhere in documents. But some questions require inference: if the documents say 'plants need sunlight' and 'the greenhouse has no windows,' a human infers no plants will survive, even though no document states that. The goal: build systems that can reason from incomplete information, deriving conclusions not explicitly written.
171.wh: Current QA systems assume the answer is 'in the corpus somewhere.' They rank documents by relevance, then extract or generate from the top ones. But inferential questions break this: the answer-supporting passages only provide clues, not the answer. You might have passage 1: 'Alice studied biology' and passage 2: 'The exam covered biology topics.' To infer 'Alice studied the exam topics,' you need to combine and reason. Standard retrievers rank by surface similarity, missing that you need both passages together. Rerankers (systems that re-order documents) help marginally, but they're still looking for explicit relevance, not inferential links.
171.ap: The paper introduces two things. First, Quit, a new dataset of 7,401 questions requiring inference from 2.4 million passages. The passages are constructed from high-convergence human and machine hints (multiple sources agreeing on clues, not the answer), labeled at three relevance levels: does this passage help, is it essential, or is it misleading? Second, they benchmark retrievers (systems that find relevant documents), rerankers (that re-order them), and LLM readers (that generate answers). This reveals what breaks: retrievers underperform (they can't recognize that two weak matches together make an inference), rerankers add little (they're still ranking by surface signals), and fine-tuning helps inconsistently.
171.ww: Why is this hard? Inference requires combining multiple pieces of evidence in a way that's not obvious from surface similarity. A retriever trained to find 'relevant passages' doesn't know that 'Alice studied X' and 'exam covers X' are separately weak but together inferentially important. The dataset construction (from convergent hints, not direct statements) forces systems to learn reasoning rather than pattern-matching. Importantly, even reasoning-oriented language models don't outperform smaller general-purpose ones, suggesting the bottleneck isn't model size—it's that current architectures don't organize the pipeline (retrieve → rerank → read) to handle inference.
171.po: The payoff is identifying a gap: current QA pipelines fail at inference-based reasoning. With the Quit dataset, researchers can now train systems specifically for this mode. Applications include legal discovery (infer from case facts), medical diagnosis (infer from symptoms and lab results), and investigative journalism (infer connections from documents).

172.bp: Imagine a search agent (an AI that autonomously searches the web across multiple turns: ask a question, read results, decide to search again or answer). These agents need to be efficient: don't waste searches, and answer as soon as you have enough information. Real goal: balance thoroughness (find the answer) with frugality (don't search unnecessarily).
172.wh: Current agents trained to get the right final answer have a perverse incentive: they search excessively because searching is free (to the training objective) and there's no penalty for wasted effort. They often do redundant searches (searching the same thing twice), or conversely, stop too early and give wrong answers. The root cause: the model was trained to optimize 'did you get the final answer right,' not 'what was the search process.' This creates misaligned decision boundaries—the threshold for 'I have enough info to answer' is wrong. Over-search wastes resources; under-search produces errors. You can't fix this by tweaking hyper-parameters because the signal itself is misaligned.
172.ap: The paper proposes causal intervention-based diagnosis and decision boundary alignment. First, diagnose: at each decision point (should I search again or answer?), compare the actual trajectory to a counterfactual ('what if I had answered now instead of searching?'). This reveals whether the agent chose correctly. Build a dataset of these 'decision points where the agent erred' (over-searched or under-searched). Then, train a preference optimizer on this dataset: the agent learns to prefer correct decisions over incorrect ones. The causal intervention part is crucial: you're not just labeling 'this trajectory was bad'; you're identifying the specific decision point that went wrong.
172.ww: This works because you're fixing the actual problem: the decision boundary. Over-search and under-search are both decision errors, and they have different causes (overconfidence in one case, premature termination in the other). By diagnosing causal counterfactuals (what would have happened if I'd decided differently), you identify exactly which decisions were wrong, not just that the overall trajectory failed. Then preference optimization teaches the agent to make better decisions going forward. The causal framing ensures you're training on the right signal—the decision itself, not noise from downstream outcomes.
172.po: On public datasets, the method reduces both over-search and under-search, improving overall efficiency. Agents answer correctly while searching fewer times. The payoff: services like search assistants or research agents that answer questions reliably without wasting computational resources.

173.bp: In social networks, relationships are complex: some ties are positive (friends, allies), others negative (rivals, blocked users). A community—a tightly-knit group—should have many positive links within and few negative links within, but may have some negative links to outsiders. Understanding these signed communities reveals conflicts and alliances. Goal: reliably cluster nodes despite the noise of conflicting edge signs.
173.wh: Real networks are messy. An edge marked 'negative' might be mislabeled (data entry error) or ambiguous (two people who cooperate on one project but compete on another). Existing community detection methods treat all conflicts equally, so noisy data creates inconsistent clusters: one run gives cluster A, another gives cluster B. The fundamental tension: do you trust an edge sign or treat it skeptically? Too trusting and noise ruins structure. Too skeptical and you lose real conflicts.
173.ap: ReCon is a post-processing framework (works on top of any community detection method). It refines communities iteratively: (1) Structural refinement: look at the detected clusters and check internal consistency—if a node is assigned to a cluster but has many negative ties within it, consider moving it. (2) Boundary refinement: focus on nodes at cluster boundaries (lots of neighbors in other clusters); decide whether they belong inside or should move. (3) Contrastive learning: within-cluster edges should be 'similar' (share properties), between-cluster edges should be dissimilar. Train to capture this. (4) Clustering: use the learned similarities to finalize cluster assignments.
173.ww: This works because it tackles both the data problem (noise) and the model problem (conflicting signals). Structural refinement directly corrects errors (noisy edge signs). Boundary refinement focuses effort on hard cases where membership is genuinely ambiguous. Contrastive learning amplifies consistent patterns: if many edges agree that two people are in the same community, the learning step strengthens that signal; if they conflict, the error gets attenuated. Because ReCon is post-processing, it's method-agnostic—you can apply it to any base community detector.
173.po: On 18 synthetic and 4 real networks using 4 different base detectors, ReCon consistently improves accuracy. The payoff: more reliable signed-network analysis in social networks (detecting polarized groups), organizational networks (identifying conflict), and biology (predicting protein interactions, where 'negative' means inhibition).

174.bp: Wearable devices and mobile sensors generate time-series data—heartbeat, step count, GPS location. These streams come from diverse devices and users. A central server wants to train one model that works for everyone, without collecting raw data (privacy). But users' devices and environments differ: some have noisy sensors, different activity types, different climate zones. The goal: federated learning (train across distributed devices) that generalizes despite this diversity.
174.wh: Standard federated learning assumes data from all users is roughly similar, just distributed. But time-series from different devices and environments violate this: a jogger's heart rate looks different from a sprinter's, sensor noise varies, seasonal patterns differ. This out-of-distribution (OOD) shift breaks generalization. Current methods try to squeeze diverse distributions into one model or compress sequences heavily, losing temporal structure. The tension: you want to account for diverse patterns, but you can't send raw data to a central server (privacy), and you can't train per-user models (that's not federated learning).
174.ap: FedDiG treats time-series from a frequency-domain perspective (breaking signals into their component frequencies, like how music has bass and treble). Each device learns a frequency-domain representation locally—a compact descriptor of 'what frequencies matter for this user.' The server collects these descriptors (not raw data), then creates a global frequency pool and uses class-wise mixup (blending different frequency patterns for the same class, like mixing tempo variations). This mixed frequency information guides a central diffusion model (a generative model that builds data from random noise by gradually refining it). The diffusion model synthesizes new time-series with diverse spectral patterns—essentially creating synthetic variations that capture OOD diversity.
174.ww: This works because frequency-domain representations are private (they're compressed summaries, not time-steps) yet informative (they capture the essential structure of each device's data). By aggregating frequency descriptors, the server learns 'what frequencies characterize each class across all devices,' then uses that to synthesize diverse examples. Diffusion models are good at generating diverse variations while respecting semantic structure (the synthesized data is recognizably 'a jog' or 'a sprint' but with different sensor profiles). Training on synthetic diversity-augmented data forces the model to be robust to OOD variation.
174.po: On four cross-domain time-series benchmarks (transferring from one device/environment to unseen others), FedDiG significantly outperforms federated learning and other domain-generalization methods. The payoff: wearable health monitoring that works across device types and user populations without centralizing private data.

175.bp: Recommender systems increasingly use pre-trained multimodal models (trained on billions of images and text) to encode item metadata—a product photo, description, reviews. These models capture rich information, but they're not tuned for your specific interests. The goal: adapt these powerful pre-trained models to recommendation without retraining them from scratch (too expensive), while personalizing to user interests (so it learns what *you* care about in images).
175.wh: Standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pre-trained models with a small number of new parameters per task—cheap and effective. But here's the catch: the adaptation is global—the same adapted model for all users. A user interested in technical details might attend to different aspects of a jacket (seam quality, material texture) than a user interested in fashion trends (color, silhouette). If you use the same item embeddings for both users, you lose that personalization—both see the same summary of the product, even though they care about different things.
175.ap: PerPEFT groups users by interest cluster (segmentation based on purchase patterns) and assigns a distinct fine-tuning module to each group. Now a 'quality-focused' group's model learns to highlight aspects predictive of quality purchases, while a 'fashion-focused' group's model highlights style aspects. The same product image is processed through the appropriate group-specific adapter, producing different embeddings for different user types. They also introduce a specialized training technique that strengthens user-group conditioning: the adapter learns to produce embeddings that diverge based on user group.
175.ww: This works because personalization and efficiency become compatible. Standard PEFT is efficient but one-size-fits-all. By segmenting users into groups with coherent interests and assigning micro-modules per group, you get personalized embeddings (different users see different aspects) with minimal added parameters (each group's module is small, and you're only adding 1.3% overall). Users in the same interest cluster have similar attention patterns, so grouping is efficient; users across clusters have different priorities, so personalization helps. The technique that strengthens conditioning ensures the adapter actually learns to differ across groups rather than converging.
175.po: Experiments show NDCG@20 (ranking quality metric) improves by up to 15.3% over strong baselines. The payoff: recommendation systems that adapt powerful multimodal models to user interests while remaining lightweight enough for real-time serving.

176.bp: Gig platforms (food delivery, task freelancing) set prices for work and wait for workers to accept. They want to minimize costs and cover all available tasks. Workers—from diverse geographies, with different financial needs—have uncertainty about their own willingness to work at a given price. The platform knows this and can exploit it. Real issue: can platforms systematically suppress wages by taking advantage of workers' uncertainty?
176.wh: In classical labor economics, the market wage would converge to equilibrium. But gig platforms have an information advantage: they know aggregate labor supply better than individual workers know their own costs. Workers uncertain about their reservation wage (the minimum they'll accept) might accept underpaying jobs. Worse, platforms can adjust pricing dynamically to learn and exploit this. If a platform posts low wages and workers keep accepting, it learns workers' uncertainty is high and keeps wages low. Standard economic models assume rational actors with full information; actual gig markets don't satisfy this.
176.ap: The paper models this as a posted-price game. A platform must cover M tasks by posting prices and waiting for workers to accept (if price exceeds their estimated cost). First, the authors show a simple strategy: post low prices initially. Because workers are uncertain about their costs, many will accept even underpriced work (they think their cost might be lower). The platform can cover all tasks while paying only O(log(M)/M) of total labor costs. Then they study collective action: if a strategic coalition of workers commits to a price floor (refusing anything below X), the platform's exploitation power vanishes. The required spending jumps from logarithmic to linear. But a random coalition of equal size is ineffective.
176.ww: This works mathematically because uncertainty is asymmetric. The platform updates its beliefs about worker willingness from observed acceptances; workers don't update fast enough individually. A small strategic coalition with commitment power shifts leverage because it removes the platform's ability to experiment: the platform can't post low prices and learn—it immediately hits the floor. The contrast between strategic and random coalitions reveals that effective collective action requires targeting the right workers (those whose rejection signals the most information to peers).
176.po: The theory is validated with synthetic experiments across market regimes. The payoff: a formal model of wage suppression in gig economies and proof that targeted collective action (unions, coordinated strategies) is necessary, not just random worker organizing. This informs policy and organizing strategy.

177.bp: Misinformation spreads online, and combating it requires understanding intent: some false claims aim to manipulate opinion, others to exploit emotions, others to distract. A single false claim might have multiple coexisting intents. Understanding intent improves detection (fact-checkers prioritize high-impact lies) and response (different intents need different debunking). Goal: model intent without hand-labeled examples (expensive) and predict veracity end-to-end.
177.wh: Existing approaches model intent as a single categorical label (this is 'emotional manipulation' or 'political distortion'), but real claims are mixed. Also, most require LLM inference for every sample, which is expensive at scale. And they struggle with the multiplicity: a claim that says 'vaccines cause autism' might simultaneously aim to scare parents and distrust authorities—one intent label misses the nuance. The challenge: model multiple intents unsupervised (no labels) and do it efficiently.
177.ap: IConMoE combines concept activation vectors with mixture-of-experts. Concept activation vectors are a method for identifying specific high-level concepts (like 'emotional language' or 'conspiracy framing') that a neural network recognizes. A mixture-of-experts layer has multiple specialized 'experts,' each focusing on different aspects, with a gating mechanism that decides which experts to trust for each input. The model learns intents in an unsupervised manner: different experts implicitly capture different intents, without needing labels. A gating layer learns to weight experts based on the claim, naturally modeling multiple coexisting intents.
177.ww: This works because the architecture naturally decomposes intent. Each expert develops a specialty (one captures emotional framing, another political alignment, etc.) through the pressure of predicting veracity. The gating mechanism forces selectivity: for a claim that's mostly emotional manipulation, the emotional expert's signal is weighted up. For a mixed claim, multiple experts contribute. Concept activation vectors make this interpretable: you can ask 'what concepts does expert 3 rely on?' and get human-readable answers. The unsupervised learning is driven by the veracity prediction task: experts that help predict truthfulness survive; those that don't get deprioritized.
177.po: On three benchmark misinformation datasets, the model outperforms baselines. The payoff: interpretable intent modeling of false claims, enabling better prioritization and response without expensive LLM inference per sample.

178.bp: Graph data comes from different sources: one company's social network, another's transaction graph, a third's citation network. Each has different structure and node attributes. You want to train a model on one graph and apply it to another without retraining. Real goal: transfer knowledge from labeled graphs to unlabeled ones, across domain shifts, without centralizing data.
178.wh: Standard domain adaptation assumes similar structure but different feature distributions. Graphs are harder: structure can differ (one is sparse, another dense), features differ, and the statistical distribution of nodes across classes varies. Multi-source adaptation is even trickier: you have multiple source graphs with different properties and want to transfer to one unlabeled target. Existing methods either focus on single-source transfer (missing complementary knowledge from multiple sources) or use complex, handcrafted architectures that are hard to analyze and adapt. The tension: leverage multiple sources without overwhelming complexity.
178.ap: CPT-GDA (Concise Propagation-Transformation pipeline for multi-source Graph Domain Adaptation) uses a dual-branch graph neural network. Both branches follow the same propagation-transformation pattern (propagate information through the graph, then transform it), but with different propagation depths. This simplicity is intentional: propagation means neighbors influence each other, transformation means learning task-specific features. Multiple sources feed into this via three optimization objectives: (1) classify nodes correctly using the learned representations, (2) align representations across source and target domains (make target look more like sources), and (3) leverage multiple sources by learning shared and source-specific knowledge.
178.ww: This works because the P-T pipeline is interpretable and effective: propagation captures graph structure, transformation captures task-specific semantics. The dual-branch design lets the model learn at different 'hops' (direct neighbors vs. distant neighbors) without explosion complexity. Multi-source learning works because the model extracts common knowledge across sources (what's universally useful) and leverages source-specific details (what each source uniquely provides). By optimizing all three objectives jointly, the model learns representations that generalize to the target domain.
178.po: On multiple graph domain-adaptation benchmarks, CPT-GDA outperforms existing methods. The payoff: transfer models across different graph domains—e.g., train on a labeled company's social network, apply to an unlabeled network from a different company, without retraining.

179.bp: Psychological counseling is moving online, and LLM-powered chatbots offer 24/7 support. But most are opaque, generic, and not grounded in established therapy practices. Real goal: build an AI counselor that follows structured therapeutic methodology, explains its reasoning, evolves through sessions with the same client, and measures outcomes rigorously.
179.wh: Therapeutic practice has deep theory—different schools (CBT focuses on thoughts, SFBT focuses on solutions, MBCT focuses on mindfulness) work for different people and phases. A good therapist does Exploration (understand the problem), Insight (connect it to patterns), and Action (change behavior). Naive LLM chatbots don't model this structure; they respond to whatever the user says without a coherent plan. Also, they're single-stage (one conversation in isolation) and weakly grounded in clinical evidence. Hard part: coordinate multiple specialized models (for different therapies) while maintaining continuity within a session and across sessions.
179.ap: XInsight orchestrates five specialized agents. (1) Exploration agent organizes client concerns into a standardized Case Conceptualization Form (structured representation of the problem). (2) Routing agent analyzes the case and selects appropriate therapy modalities (SFBT, CBT, MBCT). (3) Therapeutic agent executes school-consistent interventions (cognitive restructuring for CBT, solution-focused questions for SFBT, etc.). (4) Consolidation agent reviews progress, integrates skills learned, and plans relapse prevention. (5) Recording agent continuously converts open dialogue into standardized psychological records. All operate under a Reason-Intervene-Reflect cycle: reason about client state, intervene therapeutically, reflect on what happened.
179.ww: This works because it mirrors actual therapy. Exploration-Insight-Action is the classical therapeutic flow, proven by decades of practice. Recording standardized artifacts (conceptualization, interventions, reflections) creates continuity and accountability—the same client in session 2 can recall session 1 from structured records. Routing to modality-specific agents ensures interventions fit theory (you don't mix CBT and MBCT haphazardly; you route coherently). The Reason-Intervene-Reflect cycle keeps the model grounded in the current client state rather than drifting into generic advice. To measure success, they introduce Scale-Guided LLM Evaluation: use established clinical scales (for measuring depression, anxiety, etc.) alongside general counseling criteria.
179.po: Compared to existing multi-agent counseling systems, XInsight shows improved therapeutic paradigm alignment (follows theory better), deeper interaction, and interpretability. The payoff: transparent, accountable AI counseling that integrates multiple evidence-based therapies and measures psychological progress rigorously—suitable for clinical settings where outcomes matter.
